sessions.title: Turning Fuel Into Motion
sessions.summary: A calm account of how a common four-stroke petrol engine turns combustion pressure into rotation, how that rotation reaches the wheels, and how valves, coolant, and oil support the movement.

paragraphs.text: Imagine a simple drawing of a car, with its body made transparent and the engine resting quietly in view. There is no need to take the whole drawing in at once. For now, the picture can be small: one cylinder, one piston, and a curved shaft beneath them. We can move through that picture a little at a time, following one ordinary four-stroke petrol engine. The details belong to a familiar kind of car, rather than to every engine ever built. The scene can stay as uncomplicated as a pencil sketch, with each part appearing only when it has a place in the story.

The engine begins with energy carried in its fuel. Inside a cylinder, fuel and air take part in combustion, releasing some of that energy as heat. The hot gases exert pressure on a piston, a moving part fitted inside the cylinder. As the gases expand, they push the piston along its path. The engine's mechanical parts turn that movement into rotation, and the car's powertrain carries the rotation toward the wheels. Only part of the energy released becomes useful mechanical work. For the moment, though, we can follow that useful part, from the pressure of the gas to the movement of metal. The piston does not travel away from the engine. It moves back and forth within the same small space, returning over familiar ground while the shaft it drives continues to turn. That change from a repeated straight movement to rotation is the central shape of this story.

The cylinder gives the piston a path, and the crankshaft gives that path a repeating rhythm. During one turn of the crankshaft, the piston travels from one end of its movement to the other and then returns. Each one-way journey is called a stroke. The distance of that journey is also called the stroke, while the width across the inside of the cylinder is its bore. Together, bore and stroke describe the space swept by the piston. Add that swept space across all the cylinders, and the result is the engine's displacement. A larger displacement means a larger total swept volume, rather than a different kind of motion. In a four-stroke engine, the complete operating sequence takes four of those one-way movements, or two turns of the crankshaft. The piston can therefore pass through the same position while doing a different job on the next turn. Its location alone does not tell the entire story.

Before the mixture can burn, the engine must bring air and fuel together. Modern petrol engines have more than one way to do this. Some use port injection, supplying fuel before the air enters the cylinder. Others use direct injection, where an injector meters a fine spray of fuel into the combustion chamber itself. Some engines use both arrangements, choosing how to supply the fuel according to operating conditions. These details change the preparation of the mixture, but there is still air, fuel, and an ignition spark. An electronic control unit coordinates the fuel delivery and ignition with the engine's other systems. The spark plug provides the spark that starts combustion. It is a small event placed within a much larger sequence, like a cue that arrives at its appointed place. We can leave the particular injection arrangement in the background and return to the steady movement of the piston.

On the intake stroke, the piston moves away from the cylinder head as the intake passage admits the fresh charge. Next comes compression. The piston returns, reducing the space available to the trapped gases and raising their pressure. Near the end of compression, a spark starts combustion. The resulting hot, high-pressure gas pushes on the piston during the power stroke. A connecting rod carries this force to the crankshaft, turning the piston's back-and-forth movement into rotation. The final stroke is exhaust, when the piston returns toward the head and moves spent gases out through the exhaust passage. Then the sequence begins again. Intake, compression, power, and exhaust describe four different parts of one continuous movement. The power stroke contributes work that helps carry the mechanism through the other strokes as well. A cylinder is not receiving a fresh push from combustion throughout the whole cycle; there are intervals for bringing gases in, preparing them, and moving them out.

The passages into and out of the cylinder are controlled by valves. A valve opens to provide a route for gas and closes to seal that route. In the conventional arrangement we are picturing, rotating camshafts coordinate those movements. Each cam has a shaped lobe that lifts a valve through the mechanism between them. The shape of the lobe influences when the valve opens and how long it stays open, while its height influences how far the valve moves. Real valve timing is more fluid than four perfectly separate boxes on a diagram. Opening and closing can extend beyond the simple boundaries of a stroke, and there can be an interval when intake and exhaust valves are both open. Some engines also change their valve operation for different conditions. The four-stroke picture remains a useful outline, with these smaller adjustments taking place inside it. The valves let the engine manage the flow around the piston's repeated movement.

Now the drawing can widen from one cylinder to several. Their pistons connect to a common crankshaft, but their combustion events occur at different points in the sequence. A defined firing order arranges those contributions. While one cylinder is delivering a power stroke, another can be occupied with a different part of its cycle. The shared shaft gathers these individual movements into one rotating assembly. A flywheel attached to the crankshaft also helps smooth the motion between the separate contributions. It is a rotating mass that makes the sequence less abrupt, rather than another source of combustion. From outside, the engine can seem like a single object carrying out a single task. Within it, that task is distributed among parts that return to the same positions over and over. There is a quiet order to the drawing: several cylinders, a shared shaft, and a sequence that continues around them.

There is a useful word for the turning effect of a force: torque. It describes how a push or pull tends to rotate something about an axis. The place where the force acts matters as well as its size. A door offers a familiar picture. A push near its outer edge has a greater turning effect than the same push very close to the hinge, provided the direction is comparable. The hinge is the axis in that picture. In a rotating mechanism, force and distance from the axis have the same relationship. Torque is therefore different from a description of how fast something is already turning. It concerns the turning action being applied. We do not need a number to hold that distinction. One idea is the pace of rotation; the other is the effect of the force that acts around the axis.

Gears allow a mechanism to exchange rotational speed for turning effort. Picture a small gear driving a larger one. The small gear must make more turns for each turn of the larger gear, and the larger gear can deliver more torque. Reverse that relationship, and the output can turn faster with less torque. In an ideal mechanism, the exchange preserves the work being transferred; the gears do not create an extra supply of energy. A bicycle offers a gentle version of the same idea. Changing the combination of front and rear sprockets changes how many pedal turns correspond to a turn of the rear wheel and how much effort is needed at the pedals. The mechanism offers a choice of relationships between its input and output. That is the useful idea to carry back to the car: the engine's rotational pace and the turning effort delivered farther along the drivetrain can be connected in different proportions.

The transmission provides the next part of that path toward the wheels. In a conventional automatic transmission, a torque converter passes the engine's rotary motion into the transmission, and internal shafts, gears, and clutches establish the selected relationship at the output. From there, motion continues through the differential to the driven wheels. These names mark stages along the route, without requiring every part to be drawn in detail. We can picture the engine at one end and the road wheels at the other, with a sequence of connected components carrying rotation between them. What began as movement inside a cylinder has become an organised path through the car. The engine does its work locally, within its own housing, while the transmission and the components beyond it make that work available at the wheels. The drawing has grown, but the original small movement is still part of the picture.

Alongside that path of motion, another path carries heat. In the liquid-cooled engine we are picturing, circulating coolant absorbs heat from the engine and carries it to a radiator. The radiator transfers that heat to air passing through it. When the car is moving, its motion supplies airflow; when the car is stationary, a cooling fan can help move air through the radiator. Cooling is not an attempt to make the working engine as cold as possible. Its purpose is to help maintain a suitable operating temperature. It is a supporting process that continues alongside the movement of the pistons and shaft. The drawing can show it as a separate, gentle circuit, carrying heat away while the mechanical parts carry work onward. Motion and heat share the same engine, but they have different routes through and beyond it.

Oil has another supporting role among the moving parts. A film of oil helps lubricate surfaces that slide against one another, limiting direct contact between the metal surfaces. It also contributes to cooling, carrying away some of the heat associated with friction. These are related jobs: the oil belongs both to the story of movement and to the story of heat. Its behaviour depends partly on viscosity, the property we often describe as how thick or resistant to flow a fluid feels. In an engine, that property affects the oil film as conditions change. There is no need to choose an oil or think about a maintenance task here. It is enough to leave a small space for this quieter part of the picture, a fluid supporting the movement of solid parts. The visible pieces of the mechanism have companions that are less obvious in a simple drawing.

We can leave the drawing there, with its details in place and no need to keep looking at every one. Perhaps only the first pencil outline remains clear; perhaps the whole image has already become a little distant. Either way, there is nothing to finish examining. The picture can rest on the page, complete enough for this moment. The names can settle into the background, and the space around them can become quiet again.

paragraphs.text: The drawing can begin with a little more space around the engine this time. A few lines arrive from one side, and a few small marks sit above a single cylinder. There is no need to recall an earlier drawing or to keep track of every name. This picture can stand on its own. We will follow the preparation for combustion in a familiar kind of petrol engine, with fuel injection and an electrical spark. It is one useful example among many designs. The pace can stay gentle, with each part of the picture allowed to appear, do its small job in the story, and settle into the background again.

Air and fuel belong together in this example because combustion needs both. The fuel carries chemical energy, and burning it with air releases energy as heat. Inside the cylinder, the resulting hot gas exerts pressure on the piston. The mechanical parts then carry that push onward as rotation. Before that useful movement can take place, however, the engine has some preparation to do. It needs a fresh charge, a period of compression, and the start of combustion at a suitable point in the cycle. Afterward, the spent gas leaves and the sequence repeats. We can keep the familiar four-stroke outline very faint on the page: intake, compression, power, and exhaust. Our attention can rest on the smaller arrangements that make the combustion part possible, while the outline quietly holds their place in the larger movement.

First, consider the path taken by the air. In the electronically controlled arrangement we are picturing, a throttle valve helps regulate how much air is admitted to the engine. Its opening can be adjusted as operating demands change. The accelerator pedal provides an electrical request to the control unit, which coordinates the response. The pedal and the throttle therefore belong to a conversation carried by signals, with the valve doing its work in the air passage. We do not need to imagine every wire or every instruction. A simple opening in a passage is enough for now, with its position adjusted by the system around it. That opening has a place in preparing the cylinder charge. Other engine designs can manage their air differently, so this single drawing need not stand for every petrol engine.

Admitting air is one task; measuring it is another. One kind of air-mass meter uses a small heated element in the intake stream. Air flowing past carries heat away, changing the temperature pattern across the sensing area. The electronics use that change to provide information about the mass of air passing through. The physical movement becomes an electrical signal that the engine's controller can use. In our drawing, the sensor can remain a small mark beside the passage. It does not need to look important to contribute useful information. The useful distinction is simply between the air itself, continuing along its route, and information about that air, travelling to the controller by another route. One belongs to the moving charge; the other helps the engine prepare for it.

Pressure and temperature provide another view of the intake air. A combined sensor can report both conditions to the control unit, helping it determine an appropriate fuel quantity. Within one such pressure sensor, a tiny membrane changes shape under pressure, and that change is detected electrically. Temperature can be measured with an element whose electrical resistance varies as it warms or cools. The details are small enough to leave out of the main drawing, but they offer a quiet example of measurement. A physical condition becomes a signal. Different engines use different combinations of sensors, and we need not fit every possible arrangement to this one sketch. It is enough to picture the controller receiving information about the air, with each measurement adding a little context to the flow it is trying to manage.

Now a second path joins the picture: the supply of fuel. With port injection, the injector delivers fuel into the passage before the intake valve. The fuel mixes with the incoming air on the way into the cylinder. The injector meters the delivery, and the shape of its spray is chosen to suit the engine around it. Depending on the design and operating conditions, injection can take place before the intake valve opens or while it is open. There is room for timing within this apparently simple arrangement. The position of the injector gives the mixture part of the intake passage in which to form. We can imagine that stretch of passage as a meeting place, where two supplies come together before entering the cylinder. The sketch needs no individual droplets counted or traced; a gentle line for the fuel is enough.

Direct injection moves that meeting place inside the cylinder. Here the injector delivers fuel into the combustion chamber itself, supplied from a high-pressure fuel rail. Its job includes metering the quantity and breaking the fuel into a spray that supports mixture formation. The air still has its intake route, while the fuel reaches the chamber through this separate opening. Comparing the two arrangements does not require choosing a winner. Their names tell us where the fuel is introduced: in the intake port, or directly in the combustion chamber. Each arrangement has to work with the particular engine's shape and operating conditions. For our picture, the difference can be as small as moving the end of the fuel line from outside the intake valve to inside the cylinder. The larger story still has air and fuel being prepared for combustion.

The spark begins with another kind of preparation, this time electrical. An ignition coil contains windings that work with a magnetic field. Current in the primary winding builds that field. When the current is interrupted, the changing field induces a high voltage in the secondary winding. That voltage is used to produce the spark at the plug. We can picture the coil as a small stage between the electrical supply and the spark itself. It prepares the conditions for a brief event, while the engine continues its movement. The coil does not supply the fuel's chemical energy; its role is in providing ignition. There is no need to carry a voltage figure through the story. The relationship is enough: current, a magnetic field, a change in that field, and an electrical pulse delivered toward the plug.

The spark plug brings that pulse to a small gap between electrodes in the combustion chamber. As the voltage across the gap rises sufficiently, the gas there becomes able to conduct, and an electrical discharge crosses the space. This brief spark initiates combustion in the prepared mixture. The plug is therefore both a physical part of the chamber and the location of a carefully placed electrical event. We can leave its threaded body and insulating material as quiet shapes in the drawing, with our attention resting on the tiny gap. The spark is a beginning, rather than a supply that must continue throughout the whole burning process. Once that beginning has been established, the story moves outward into the surrounding mixture. A very small region has introduced a change that will develop through a much larger part of the chamber.

Normal spark-ignition combustion takes time to spread. A flame begins near the plug and travels through the mixture, rather than the entire charge burning at one perfectly simultaneous instant. Its progress takes a short interval measured in milliseconds, while the engine's mechanical motion continues. That interval is small in an everyday sense, yet it matters within a rapidly repeating cycle. We can slow the imaginary drawing without changing the real process: a small beginning, an expanding region of burning mixture, and more of the charge becoming involved. This is an outline of normal flame propagation, with the more complicated details left outside the frame. There is no need to see a dramatic flash. A gradual change across a small chamber is a useful enough picture, and it gives the timing of the original spark a clear place in the story.

To place events within the cycle, the controller needs information about the engine's movement. A crankshaft sensor provides information about rotational speed and position. Those signals help coordinate fuel injection and ignition with the turning mechanism. Speed describes how quickly the movement is repeating, while position identifies a place within that movement. The two ideas belong together without being identical. We can picture a circular outline with a small reference mark beside it: the circle supplies an image of repetition, and the mark supplies an image of location. The real sensor turns mechanical movement into an electrical signal, using a reference pattern associated with the shaft. We do not need to follow each passing feature. It is enough to leave a link between the shaft and the controller, carrying the information needed to place other events around the rotation.

The electronic engine control unit brings these separate tasks into coordination. It manages functions that include the air supply, fuel injection, and ignition, using information from the engine's sensors. The word control can sound larger than the picture needs. Here, it can mean arranging the actions of several components so that they belong to the same operating sequence. The throttle has one task, the injector another, and the ignition system another again. Their commands are related because they serve the same engine. In our sketch, a few thin signal lines can connect the parts without covering the page. The controller is not an extra source of mechanical power. Its contribution is to organise the preparation and timing around the engine's working parts. The movement remains in the cylinder and crankshaft, with this quieter network helping the individual events agree.

There is also information returning from the exhaust. An oxygen sensor, often called a lambda sensor, measures residual oxygen in the exhaust gas. Its signal allows the fuel-control system to respond to the mixture that has actually burned, rather than relying only on information gathered before combustion. The exhaust therefore has a place in a feedback loop as well as a route away from the cylinder. We can draw one more thin line returning toward the controller, with no need to add a number or an ideal ratio. The details of the system vary with the engine and its operating conditions. For this picture, the useful idea is the return of information. Something happens in the cylinder, a measurement follows downstream, and that measurement helps guide the preparation for further cycles. The drawing has gently folded back toward its beginning.

That is enough detail for this page. Perhaps the thin lines remain visible, or perhaps only the space around them feels worth noticing now. Nothing needs to be recalled in order. There is no task waiting at the edge of the drawing and no final question to answer. We can let the names become less distinct, as if the pencil had grown lighter toward the end of the sketch. The page can stay where it is, with room around it, and the rest of this moment can belong to quiet.
